The pairing table separates two opposite effects of C:
- Freed loops: 47 problems that were cut in the original now finish, and their accuracy rose from 2.1% to 19.1% (+8 correct). So breaking a loop often does let the model reach the answer.
- Already-finishing problems: on the 169 that finished under both models, accuracy fell from 29.0% to 26.0% (-5). Of the 11 that are newly cut, 2 correct answers were lost.

The net is about zero. The loss on finishing answers could be noise from token drift (roughly ±2.6 points on 169 items) or real damage. One concrete mechanism would be C pushing the model to stop or skip steps early: mean length fell from 361 to 282 tokens, and an anti-repetition push might also suppress legitimate restating of intermediate values.

So I'll compare, within the both-finished group, the lengths and line counts of edited versus original answers, separately for pairs that stayed correct and pairs that went right→wrong. If the edited answers on right→wrong pairs are clearly shorter, with fewer lines, C is truncating reasoning, which suggests a weaker β or fewer layers. If lengths match, the losses look like drift noise.

Within the answers that finished under both models, C turned 9 correct answers wrong and 4 wrong answers correct. The two right→wrong examples suggest a plausible cost. In one, the edited answer stopped after computing Billy's amount (125) and skipped the final step that re-combines earlier quantities (B + S = 200). An anti-repetition push can also discourage legitimately restating earlier values. That is suggestive only, with n = 9. Lengths and line counts otherwise match, so C doesn't broadly truncate reasoning.

The most promising use of C is the combination planned earlier. S moves problems into plain mode, which reasons better but loops more (cut 22.7% → 40% on switched problems). C frees loops, and on freed loops accuracy jumped from 2% to 19%. Their benefits should add, and the cost of C is partly offset by the loops S creates. I'll compose the two edits on the overlapping tensors: S as saved in /work/best_S1, then C(-1.5) applied on top, W' = W_S + 1.5·v vᵀW_S in layers 16 to 22. The combination is then tested with a paired generation on dev_b1, where S alone gave +1.6. A gain clearly above S alone, say +4 or more, would support stacking. A gain at or below +1.6 would mean the costs cancel.

The combined edit SC is saved: S(1.0) on layers 16 to 19 composed with C(-1.5) on layers 16 to 22, 14 tensors in all. This paired generation on dev_b1, where S alone gave +1.6 ± 2.4, tests whether freeing the loops lets S's plain-mode reasoning gain add up.

The combination is the first candidate with a sizeable effect:

| | Original | SC |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy on dev_b1 | 19.5% | 24.2% |
| Cut at max tokens | 28.5% | 20.3% |

The paired gain is +4.7 ± 2.6 points (29 wrong→right, 17 right→wrong). On the same problems S alone gave +1.6, in a separate pass, so that comparison is loose. The pattern fits the hypothesis: S moves problems into the more accurate plain mode, and C frees part of the extra loops this creates. This is a single set at about 1.8 standard errors, and dev_b1 was used to pick S, so I'll confirm on dev_b2 next. There C alone gave +0.4 and S has never been run. I'll back the candidate up as /work/best_SC first. A gain of about +3 or more on dev_b2 would support SC as a real improvement worth tuning and then freezing for HOLDOUT. A gain near zero would mean the dev_b1 result was largely noise.
